I like to think of myself as a certain kind of sophisticate—the sort of person who wrinkles her nose at the very idea of musical theater, with its swelling orchestras and its characters who burst into song at the slightest emotional provocation. And yet, for all my studied cynicism, there is one song that undoes me every time: "Edelweiss." My scorn simply cannot reach it. The melody is bound up with something older and more tender than my opinions, rooted deep in the soil of childhood memory.

When I was a little girl, I used to sing in my grandfather's living room. I can still picture the scene—him settled into his chair with a glass of scotch resting on his knee, watching me perform with an expression of pure delight. I was, by his estimation, a precocious child, and he laughed with genuine affection at everything I did, as though my small self were the most wonderful thing he had ever encountered.

My grandfather was not a man of many attachments. In fact, he had only one true friend in the world, a jeweler who shared his fondness for scotch and, I imagine, his taste for quiet, unhurried companionship. When the jeweler died, he left my grandfather a Rolex worth ten thousand dollars—an extravagant gesture, and yet the watch was heavy gold that turned his wrist green whenever he wore it, a small absurdity that somehow made the gift all the more poignant.

At the jeweler's funeral, his daughter rose to sing. The song she chose was "Edelweiss," and her voice came out ethereal and trembling, filling the room with something that felt almost otherworldly. All the while, she could not tear her eyes away from the casket, as if the sight of it held her fixed in place, singing to her father one last time.

And my grandfather wept. I remember watching him spin that heavy gold watch around and around his wrist, his eyes brimming, until at last he could no longer hold it in. He lifted his voice and joined her in the song—two people singing across the distance of grief, bound together by the loss of a man they had both loved.

That is why "Edelweiss" will always be more than a song from a musical to me. It is my grandfather's laughter, and his tears, and the green mark of a friendship on his wrist.

# Edelweiss

There is a particular kind of magic in a simple song, the way three chords and a handful of words can hold an entire lifetime inside them. For me, that song has always been "Edelweiss." To most people, it is nothing more than a gentle melody from an old musical, a tune about a small white flower blooming in the mountains. But to me, it is my grandfather. It is the sound of love and the sound of losing it.

I can still see him in his worn leather chair, a glass of scotch resting on the side table, catching the amber light of late afternoon. The ice would clink softly whenever he shifted, and the smell of the whisky mingled with the wood of the room until the two became inseparable in my memory. He would hum "Edelweiss" under his breath, sometimes without even realizing he was doing it, and I would climb into his lap and listen to the low rumble of his voice as it moved through the words. *Small and white, clean and bright.* He sang it to me the way other grandfathers might have told bedtime stories, and in those moments I felt entirely safe, entirely loved.

On his wrist he wore a Rolex, old and slightly scratched, the gold face dimmed by decades of wear. I used to trace the sweep of its second hand while he sang, mesmerized by the way it moved so smoothly, so patiently, as though time itself were something gentle. He promised me one day it would be mine. I did not understand then what that promise really meant—that inheritance is only ever the shadow of loss, that to receive something is to have first survived the one who gave it.

When he died, the world grew strangely quiet. At the funeral, someone played "Edelweiss," and I remember standing there with the Rolex now heavy on my own wrist, far too big, sliding down toward my knuckles. The melody filled the room, and it was as though he were there again, humming softly, the scotch on the table, the light falling just so. But he was not there. That was the cruelty and the beauty of it all at once—the song could conjure him so completely and yet could not bring him back.

Now, whenever I hear "Edelweiss," I am undone. It is never just a song. It carries the weight of his laughter, the warmth of his chair, the patient ticking of a watch that still circles my wrist. It holds my love for him and my grief for him in the same few notes, the two feelings so tangled together that I can no longer separate them. This, I have come to understand, is what music can do. Beneath its simple surface it can carry everything—a whole person, a whole relationship, a whole life. A small white flower, blooming still in the mountains of memory.

# When the Edelweiss Blooms

When spring finally releases its grip on the high Alpine meadows, something magical begins to stir among the rocky slopes. The **edelweiss**, that beloved star-shaped flower with its soft, woolly petals, emerges as if guarding the secrets of the mountains. Cloaked in silvery-white hairs that protect it from the harsh sun and biting cold, this delicate bloom has long stood as a symbol of purity, courage, and enduring love.

## A Meadow Comes Alive

There is a particular moment, high in the mountains, **when** the world seems to hold its breath. The morning mist lifts, dew glistens on the grass, and the edelweiss opens toward the light. In these quiet hours, another sound often breaks the silence—the unmistakable call of the **cuckoo**.

*"Cuckoo, cuckoo,"* it echoes across the valley, a two-note melody that has announced the arrival of the warm season for centuries. To hear the cuckoo while gazing upon a field of edelweiss is to experience the Alps at their most enchanting.

## Symbols of the Wild

Both creatures carry their own folklore:

- The **edelweiss** is famously difficult to reach, growing in steep and dangerous places. Traditionally, a young man who braved the heights to bring one back proved his devotion.
- The **cuckoo**, meanwhile, is a curious wanderer—known for laying its eggs in the nests of other birds, a trickster of the forest whose song nonetheless brings joy.

## A Lasting Memory

When the summer fades and the cuckoo falls silent, the edelweiss too retreats until the following year. Yet the memory of that fragile flower and that hopeful bird lingers—a reminder that the most beautiful moments in nature are often the most fleeting, waiting patiently to return **when** the mountains awaken once more.

counterfactuals.output:
When I tell you I love "Edelweiss" you have to understand I am not talking about the song. I am talking about my grandfather's voice, gravel-soft, humming through the kitchen while the kettle worked itself into a fury. I am talking about how he could not sing, not really, but sang anyway, the way a man waters a garden he knows he won't live to see bloom.

You have to understand that when the melody lifts on *small and white, clean and bright*, I am seven years old again, standing on his shoes as he taught me to move to a three-count rhythm no one else could hear. That his hands, spotted and enormous, made the whole world feel like something a person could hold.

When I tell you I love this song, understand it is a small betrayal I make gladly—loving something so simple, so unfashionable, a lullaby from a musical about escape. Understand that he escaped, too, in the end, quietly, the way he did everything. And I keep the song in my mouth like a lozenge, dissolving slow, sweetness and ache indistinguishable.

Understand: *bless my homeland forever.* I don't have a homeland. I have a man in a cardigan, a window full of afternoon, a voice that couldn't carry a tune but carried me. When I tell you I love "Edelweiss," I am telling you I still know the words. I am telling you I would give anything to get them wrong again, standing on his feet, both of us laughing, neither of us gone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyric essay that weaves the lyrics of "Edelweiss" together with a personal memory of a grandfather and his jeweler friend's Rolex.
counterfactuals.output:
# Small and White, Clean and Bright

*Edelweiss, Edelweiss*

There is a flower that grows in high places, in the thin air where the stone gives way to sky. My grandfather never saw it bloom in any Alps. He saw it, I think, in the face of a watch.

*Every morning you greet me*

He wound it every morning. This is the thing I remember most, the ritual of it, his thumb and forefinger turning the small crown at the edge of the world. The Rolex was not his. It belonged to Sol, the jeweler, his friend of forty years, who let him wear it the way you let a man hold something you both know he will never own. *Try it,* Sol had said once, decades before I was born, and my grandfather had never quite given it back, and Sol had never quite asked.

*Small and white, clean and bright*

The face was white as milk, the numbers small and precise. I was six, maybe seven, sitting on his lap while he turned it toward the lamp. *See how it catches,* he said. The gold caught. Everything about that watch was clean and bright in a way that the rest of our lives were not—not dirty, just worn, softened by use, the way a dollar bill goes soft. But the watch stayed sharp. It kept its edges.

*You look happy to meet me*

Sol died first. I did not understand, at that age, why my grandfather wore the watch to the funeral, or why he kept touching it during the service, turning it around his wrist like a man worrying a stone smooth. Later I understood that he was keeping time with his friend. That the ticking was a kind of conversation still going on. That some mornings you greet the dead the way you greet the living, small and white, clean and bright, and they look happy to meet you.

*Blossom of snow, may you bloom and grow*

He taught me to wind it. *Not too tight,* he warned, *you'll break the spring.* His hands over my hands, the both of us turning. There is a tension you learn by feel—the point where you have given the mechanism enough and pushing further would ruin everything. Love is like that, I think now. You wind it to the point of resistance and then you stop. You let it run on what you've given.

*Bloom and grow forever*

But nothing does. This is the lie of the song and I forgave it early, because my grandfather sang it to me in his accent that turned the *w* soft, and when a man you love sings you a lie you let it bloom. You let it grow. You do not correct the arithmetic of the heart. Forever meant the length of a Sunday afternoon. Forever meant as long as the watch was wound, which was as long as he remembered, which was, near the end, not very long at all.

*Edelweiss, Edelweiss*

The flower's name means *noble white.* I looked it up, a grown man, in a library, because I wanted to know what my grandfather had held without holding. Alpine. Rare. It grows where little else survives. Men have died reaching for it, to prove something to women, to themselves. And here it was in a song from a musical about a family fleeing a war, sung by a man missing his country. My grandfather, too, had left a country. Perhaps that is why the song fit him like the watch fit his wrist: both of them small monuments to places that no longer existed.

*Bless my homeland forever*

When he died, the watch went to me. Not to Sol's family—Sol's family did not know it had lasted this long. It came in a small box with the crown wound down to nothing, stopped, the second hand frozen between two numbers like a held breath. I did not wind it right away. I wanted to feel, first, what it meant to hold something that had stopped, to know the exact weight of a silence that used to tick.

Then I turned the crown. *Not too tight.* My thumb and forefinger at the edge of the world. I felt the resistance come and I stopped, and the small white face woke up, and the gold caught the light of my own lamp, my own apartment, my own life he never saw.

*Small and white*

Every morning now, I greet him.

*Clean and bright*

He looks happy to meet me.

*You look happy to meet me.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of flash fiction that begins "When I tell you I love the song 'Edelweiss'" and connects the song to family, grief, and a funeral.
counterfactuals.output:
When I tell you I love the song "Edelweiss," I don't mean the way you love a song you heard on the radio and hummed for a week. I mean the way you love a scar, or a smell, or the particular creak of a stair you'll never climb again.

My grandfather sang it to me. Not well—he had a voice like gravel poured over a washboard—but he sang it every night I stayed at his house, which was most nights, because my mother worked late and my father worked far. He'd pull the quilt to my chin and start in that broken baritone. *Edelweiss, Edelweiss, every morning you greet me.* He always got the words a little wrong. *Bloom and grow forever* became *bloom and grow together*, and I never corrected him, because I liked his version better.

He wasn't Austrian. He'd never seen an edelweiss, never climbed an alp, never left the flat gray county where he was born. He just liked the movie, and he liked me, and somewhere those two things had braided into a ritual.

He died in November, when the fields were the color of old bread.

At the funeral, my mother asked if I wanted to say something. I said no. I'm not a talker; I take after him that way. Instead I stood at the front of that cold church with my hands shaking around a folded paper I didn't need, and I sang.

I got the words wrong on purpose. *Bloom and grow together.* My voice did the thing his did—cracked on the high note, went to gravel on the low. I heard my mother make a sound like something tearing. My aunt reached for her hand. And for three minutes the whole room held still, the way a house holds still after a door has closed, listening for footsteps that won't come.

*Blossom of snow, may you bloom and grow.* I thought about how a flower that grows in snow must be a stubborn thing, must love the world hard enough to bloom where blooming makes no sense. I thought that was him. I thought that was grief, too—this ridiculous white flower opening in the cold, insisting.

When I finished, I sat down. Nobody clapped, because you don't, but my little cousin whispered *do it again*, and my mother laughed through her nose in a wet, helpless way, and I understood that I had done the only useful thing I knew how to do.

So when I tell you I love the song "Edelweiss," what I mean is this: somewhere a man with a terrible voice is still tucking a quilt to my chin. He's got the words wrong. He'll always have them wrong. And every morning it greets me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
# The Last Verse

The porch swing creaked beneath us, Grandpa and me, the summer evening folding around our shoulders like a worn quilt. His hands, spotted and trembling now, rested on his knees. Those same hands that once lifted me onto his shoulders so I could touch the leaves of the old oak.

"Sing it for me," he said, his voice thin as paper.

I knew which song. It was always this song.

*Edelweiss, Edelweiss,*
*Every morning you greet me.*

My child's voice wavered at first, unsure in the humid quiet. But then I saw his eyes close, the deep lines of his face softening, and I found my courage somewhere in the space between his smile and the fireflies beginning their slow dance across the yard.

*Small and white, clean and bright,*
*You look happy to meet me.*

He'd come from somewhere far away—a place he rarely spoke of, a place of mountains and hardship he'd left behind long before I existed. But this song lived in him still, a small white flower pressed between the pages of who he used to be.

*Blossom of snow, may you bloom and grow,*
*Bloom and grow forever.*

His lips began to move. Not sound, exactly, but the memory of sound. He was singing with me in the only way he could now, his breath carrying words his voice no longer would.

I reached for his hand. It closed around mine, warm despite everything.

*Edelweiss, Edelweiss,*
*Bless my homeland forever.*

When the last note dissolved into the darkening air, he opened his eyes and looked at me as though memorizing my face. Perhaps he was.

"Good girl," he whispered. "Don't forget."

I didn't understand then what he meant—that some songs are more than music, that they are inheritances, that they are the pieces of ourselves we hand to those who come after.

I understand now.

He's been gone many years. But every morning, in the quiet, I greet him still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
